extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary biography and 18th-century literary history
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative observations relevant to producing or judging literary biography and related forms (travel writing, club reportage, memoir), drawn from a critical/biographical essay on Boswell. Focuses on qualities such as veracity, authorial presence, style, and documentary value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veracity in travel writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Any fool may write a most valuable book by chance, if he will only tell us what he heard and saw _with veracity_.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay cites Gray's remark approving Boswell's Corsica account: truthful reporting of observed facts (what one heard and saw) is a principal source of a travel book's value. Example: readers trusted Boswell because he 'could invent nothing of the kind.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensible orthography/style choices
rubrics_metrics.description: The peculiar orthography of the writer is defended in the preface, for he allows himself not only such divergency as 'tremenduous,' 'authour,' 'ambassadour,' but also 'authentick' and 'panegyrick.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonstandard spellings or stylistic oddities can be acceptable when explicitly defended by the author in a preface; the authorial defense contextualizes and legitimizes eccentric orthography as a conscious choice rather than error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of personal publicity / first‑hand chronicling
rubrics_metrics.description: He was a most assiduous chronicler of his own actions, and there can be no doubt that there is much Boswell 'copy' buried in the pages of the papers of the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active self-reporting (press paragraphs, contributions to periodicals) builds reputation and provides first-hand material; this method of obtaining first-hand information is a legitimate tactic for the literary self-fashioning of a public figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek consent before publishing private correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: He flew to obtain the approval of his labours and, with an eye to all future contingencies, his sanction for the publication _in his biography_ of all Johnson's letters to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The anecdote (and Johnson's reluctant reply: 'When I am dead, sir, you may do as you will.') highlights the ethical/procedural norm of securing a subject's permission before publishing private letters; failing to do so may give offence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biographer's presence / authorial intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The _Life of Johnson_, as we shall indicate in its proper place, is no less the life of the biographer, whose mind was ever seeking to shelter itself under the guidance of a stronger force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware that a biography can become as much the story of the biographer as of the subject; biographers' self-insertion, their need for moral anchorage, or their personal agenda can shape and skew the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour's uneven critical reception
rubrics_metrics.description: The rollicking humour of Bozzy in this his first book was sealed to the recluse critic who 'never spoke out.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humorous or rollicking styles may appeal to a broad readership but be missed or undervalued by more reclusive/fastidious critics; authors should be aware that tone affects which audiences will appreciate the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity in persona/character pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: It is thought [his verses] are well suited to the occasion, while at the same time they preserve the true Corsican character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing in a persona (e.g., a Corsican chief), preserve an authentic or convincing sense of character appropriate to the occasion; faithful characterization strengthens occasional verse and dramatic reportage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality norms for private clubs/societies
rubrics_metrics.description: That charge we can believe Forster to be right in suspecting to be a caution against publishing abroad the proceedings and the talk of the members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership in private literary clubs carries an expectation of discretion; authors and chroniclers should treat club talk and proceedings as potentially confidential unless explicitly cleared for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of biographical bias and rivalry
rubrics_metrics.description: Boswell shews ever a curious depreciation of Goldsmith. Rivalry for the good graces of their common friend Johnson... made him suspicious of the merits of the poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal rivalries, competition for patronage or favor, and the biographer's own relationships can introduce bias; readers and writers should account for these distortions when assessing character portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentary thoroughness secures posterity
rubrics_metrics.description: Without his record the fame of that club would have passed away... apart from the record of Boswell, [many members] would be but names to the literary antiquary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed records, memoirs, or biographies preserve the reputations and achievements of otherwise forgettable figures; thorough documentation is a key contribution of biographical work to posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success as index of substantive qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The book ran to a third edition before the October of the same year. As purchased by the Dillys for a hundred guineas it would appear to have been a profitable speculation, and the wide circulation to which it attained we shall see was not merely due to accident but to more solid qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sales, multiple editions, and wide circulation may reflect genuine merits of a work (not only chance); commercial reception can serve as one indicator of substantive quality, though not the sole test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive pietistic/moralizing commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Boswell often indicates the decline and fall of the moralist by an apparently undue vein of pietistic comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An overabundance of pietistic or moralizing remarks can undermine credibility and suggest compensatory motives; moderation preserves persuasive force and avoids signaling moral decline in the narrator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid descriptive detail and dialogue in reportage
rubrics_metrics.description: He had a free hand as a writer for the London Magazine... he contributed the following account, accompanied with a portrait... 'One of the most remarkable masks upon this occasion was James Boswell, Esq., in the dress of an armed Corsican chief.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rich, scene-setting description (costume, dialogue, specific actions) and inclusion of portraiture lend liveliness and authority to festival/masquerade reporting; such concrete detail engages readers and supports the piece's vividness.
